C1.text: A partner's perceived fairness of the allocation is predicted by comparison referents, entitlement and justifications (distributive justice framework), not by the actual split alone: a partner who carries the larger share can perceive the allocation as fair.

C2.text: A partner's perceived fairness of the allocation predicts that partner's relationship satisfaction better than the actual split does, and the split's effect on satisfaction runs through perceived fairness.

C3.text: Each partner over-claims their own contribution, so the two partners' self-reported shares of chores add to more than the whole, and an allocation cannot rest on each partner's unaided recall of who does what.

C4.text: Perceived fairness depends on burden, not on count or duration of chores alone: which chores are done, how they are experienced, cognitive labour and the partner's other demands shape whether an allocation is judged fair.

C5.text: Perceived fairness has been measured by a small number of recurring instruments (global single-item fairness, multi-item scales, referent-specific or self-versus-partner items); the measure chosen changes what is found.

C6.text: Under equity theory, perceived inequity arises both for the under-benefited and the over-benefited partner, and the under-benefited partner's distress is larger; both partners' perceived fairness matters for the couple.
